etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle Dutch grabben (“to grab”) or Middle Low German grabben (“to snap”), from Old Dutch or Old Saxon gravan, from Proto-West Germanic *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grab-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ-.

See also Sanskrit गृह्णाति (gṛhṇā́ti), गृभ्णाति (gṛbhṇā́ti, “he seizes”), Avestan 𐬔𐬭𐬀𐬠 (grab, “to seize”)). Cognate with Danish grabbe (“to grab”), Swedish grabba (“to grab”), Old English ġegræppian (“to seize”), Middle English grappen (“to feel with the hands; grope”), Macedonian грабне (grabne, “to snatch”), Bulgarian грабя (grabja, “to rob, to grab”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To grip suddenly; to seize; to clutch.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Old Applegate, in the stern, just set and looked at me, and Lord James, amidship, waved both arms and kept hollering for help. I took a couple of everlasting big strokes and managed to grab hold of the skiff's rail, close to the stern.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make a sudden grasping or clutching motion (at something).
(transitive) To grip the attention of; to enthrall or interest.

quote.citation: 1992, “The Sidewinder Sleeps Tonite”, in Automatic for the People, performed by R.E.M.:
quote.text: Baby, instant soup doesn't really grab meToday I need something more substantial

definitions.definition: (informal) To quickly collect, retrieve, or take.

quote.citation: 1987, James Grady, Just a Shot Away, Bantam, page 117:
quote.text: "I'll just grab my jacket," said Manh-Hung.

quote.citation: 1999, Jillian Dagg, Racing Hearts, Thomas Bouregy & Co., page 105:
quote.text: Hardly believing that Rafe actually planned to relax for a while, Kate nodded. "All right. Fine. I'll just go grab my purse."

quote.citation: 2009, Mike Taylor, A Thousand Sleeps,, Tate Publishing, page 216:
quote.text: He looked at Albert and Ben, and then back to Nurse Allen. "I'll just grab my gear and be right back."

quote.citation: 2012 May 19, Paul Fletcher, “Blackpool 1-2 West Ham”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: Both teams wasted good opportunities to score but it was the London side who did grab what proved to be the decisive third when the unmarked Vaz Te, a January signing from Barnsley, drilled the ball into the net from 12 yards.

quote.citation: 1931 April, Harold M. Sherman, “The Baseball Clown”, in Boys' Life, volume 21, number 4, Boy Scouts of America, page 47:
quote.text: The ball popped in and popped out, and when he made a grab for it on the ground he kicked it with his foot.

quote.citation: 2003, J Davey, Six Years of Darkness, Trafford Publishing, page 66:
quote.text: He made a grab for me and I swung my handbag at him as hard as I could.

definitions.definition: (countable) An acquisition by violent or unjust means.
A device for withdrawing drills, etc., from artesian and other wells that are drilled, bored, or driven.
(countable) A mechanical device that grabs or clutches.

quote.citation: 1945 January and February, T. F. Cameron, “Dock Working”, in Railway Magazine, page 11:
quote.text: Almost all modern cranes are electrically operated and a quick-acting type of 30 cwt. capacity is suitable for general cargo, but not powerful enough to operate grabs for discharge of bulk cargoes.

quote.citation: 2008, Melissa Agnew, Here is the (Australian) News:
quote.text: For example, one radio bulletin may feature one central issue, like a state election, and will focus on that issue. The bulletin might contain only a few voice wraps but many grabs, leaving the focus firmly on the newsreader.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Arabic غُرَاب (ḡurāb) and Hindi ghurb?: crow, raven, a kind of Arab ship. This etymology is incomplete. You can help Wiktionary by elaborating on the origins of this term.

definitions.definition: A two- or three-masted vessel used on the Malabar coast.
